note.question: How can evaluating the efficacy of providers’ compensation contracts in improving participant retention support clinical studies?
note.overview: In this work, we aim to analyze a clinical study sponsor’s decisions regarding monetary payments to participants and compensation for providers (investigators and coordinators) for their efforts to improve participant retention in the study. To this end, we first consider a centralized model where the sponsor decides the monetary payments to participants and the providers’ efforts. We then identify the optimal contracts for the providers under the two decentralized team structures: the sponsor-investigator (SI) model and the outsourcing (OM) model.

source.quote: In this work, we aim to analyze a clinical study sponsor’s decisions regarding monetary payments to participants and compensation for providers (investigators and coordinators) for their efforts to improve participant retention in the study.

For example, Jain et al. (2013) developed contracts based on the performance of repairs in the context of after-sale service, Hasija et al. (2008) and Feng et al. (2019) developed performance/ outcome-based contracts contingent on the agent types in the context of the call center, Zhang et al. (2018) con­ sidered contracts based on the outcome and the reported efforts by the provider in a general service set­ ting.
One common aspect of this literature is that the principal does not observe agents’ efforts, whereas, as discussed in the Introduction, the providers’ efforts are observable in our setting.
Here, the sponsor, the investigator, and the coordinator belong to the same organization, and the sponsor knows the providers’ type.

Furthermore, Tian et al. (2021, 2023) considered the dropout rate to be an exoge­ nous random variable, whereas we consider that the retention rate depends on the efforts of the providers and the monetary incentive offered by the sponsor.
For theoretical completeness and to show the robustness of our insights, in Online Appendix EC.5.3, we analyze a setting where the sponsor does not ob­ serve the providers’ true efforts.
Note that, depend­ ing on the clinical study team structures, the sponsor may or may not know the providers’ type.
